tagline: A gravel road crosses dolomite glades above Missouri’s rolling Ozark country.
intro: Glade Top Trail follows narrow Ozark ridges approximately 500 feet above the surrounding countryside. Its 23 miles are two-lane gravel, passing grassland openings and woods. Designated a National Forest Scenic Byway in 1989, it takes its name from the glades along the ridges. The Forest Service describes seven overlooks with views reaching northwest to the Springfield Plateau and south to Arkansas’s Boston Mountains.

The Civilian Conservation Corps worked on the road in the late 1930s, but its exact contribution is uncertain. Mark Twain National Forest’s historical files suggest that a 1935 map shows an earlier road or trail along part of the route; the extent of CCC reconstruction is unclear. A 1940 forest map shows a road along the present route. Quarried-stone culverts and retaining walls occur along a road that has changed little in appearance since the 1930s.

From Ava, approach by Highways 5 and A through Smallett Junction to the first stop, Hayden Park. Arkansas View and Caney Day Use Area follow in the numbered stop sequence. Continue on Forest Road 147 to Longrun, or take the branch on Forest Road 149 to Highway 125. Between stops, dolomite outcrops and shallow soils support the grasses and wildflowers that give the road its name.
notice: Look for open grassland and exposed rock between the wooded stretches.

moments.title: Hayden Park
moments.text: Hayden Park is the first stop when approaching from Ava by way of Smallett Junction. Picnic tables mark a pause before continuing on A409 toward Forest Road 147. Beyond this entrance, the byway follows narrow ridges through glades and woodland. The road itself is part of the scene: two lanes of gravel, with quarried-stone culverts and retaining walls in places, and little change in appearance since the 1930s.

moments.title: Arkansas View
moments.text: A picnic table and horse hitch furnish Arkansas View, stop three on Glade Top Trail. The byway’s seven overlooks collectively offer views toward the Springfield Plateau and the Boston Mountains in Arkansas. The openings along the route deserve attention too. Glades are grasslands with shallow soils and exposed rock; dolomite is the principal bedrock here. Its calcium-rich soils help determine which grasses and wildflowers grow. The Forest Service compares the glades’ rocky, largely shadeless conditions with desert environments. Roadrunners, collared lizards, tarantulas and scorpions inhabit these glades.

moments.title: Caney Day Use Area
moments.text: Caney Day Use Area places its picnic ground on an Ozark glade. A hard-packed dirt path leads from the parking area to tables on a concrete pad; rock steps descend to an amphitheater with wooden benches. The Forest Service singles out Caney for scenery and plant viewing. From spring through fall, the trail and Caney Picnic Area offer opportunities to see coneflowers, Missouri primrose, prairie roses and milkweed. These grassland openings sit within a wider patchwork of woods and glades. Prescribed fire and other restoration practices help maintain glade habitat in the Ava area.

practical: Hayden Park: The byway is gravel. ATV and UTV riders need a county permit. No stops have drinking water. (checked 2026-10-11)
